title: 5. Insolvency of Partners
subtitle: Garner vs Murray, Insolvency of All Partners, Piecemeal Distribution, Proportionate Capital Method, Maximum Loss Method

questions.q: A partner is said to be "insolvent" when:
options: The partner is unable to pay their private debts and the amount due to the firm, as adjudicated by a competent court
The partner retires from the firm
The partner merely has a temporary cash shortage
The partner's capital account shows a credit balance

questions.q: When an insolvent partner is unable to bring in the deficiency in their Capital Account, the resulting loss is known as a:
options: Goodwill adjustment
Revaluation surplus
Capital deficiency
Realisation profit

questions.q: The rule laid down in Garner vs Murray relates to:
options: How solvent partners should bear the loss arising from a co-partner's insolvency
How a retiring partner's dues should be settled
How a Joint Life Policy should be accounted for
How goodwill should be valued on admission

questions.q: Under the Garner vs Murray rule, the deficiency caused by an insolvent partner's inability to pay is borne by the solvent partners:
options: In the ratio of their capitals, as last agreed or standing before the dissolution
In the ratio of their drawings
In their profit-sharing ratio
Equally, regardless of capital or profit-sharing ratio

questions.q: The Garner vs Murray rule applies:
options: Only to firms with exactly two partners
Even if the partnership deed expressly provides a different method
Only in the absence of an agreement between partners specifying a different basis
Only when the insolvent partner is the most senior partner

questions.q: Under the Garner vs Murray rule, a solvent partner whose own Capital Account already shows a debit balance is:
options: Not required to bear a share of the insolvent partner's deficiency
Still required to bear a proportionate share, regardless of their own deficit
Entitled to receive compensation from the insolvent partner
Required to bear double the normal share

questions.q: The rationale for excluding a solvent partner with a debit capital balance from bearing the insolvency loss is that:
options: Such partners are legally exempt by statute from all partnership obligations
Such partners never share in profits
A person who cannot themselves pay cannot reasonably be asked to contribute to another's deficiency
Such partners are always the most senior

questions.q: When all the partners of a firm become insolvent, the situation is referred to as:
options: Partial dissolution
Insolvency of the firm
Compulsory amalgamation
Voluntary winding up

questions.q: When all partners are insolvent, the firm's creditors are paid:
options: Out of whatever amount is realised from the firm's assets, on a pro-rata basis if insufficient
Only out of the partners' private estates
In full, regardless of the amount realised
Not at all, as the firm ceases to have obligations

questions.q: "Piecemeal distribution" refers to a situation where, on dissolution:
options: The firm's assets are realised gradually over time, and cash is distributed among partners as it becomes available
Distribution is postponed indefinitely until all partners agree
Only the insolvent partner receives any payment
All assets are realised and distributed in a single instalment

questions.q: Piecemeal distribution is necessary mainly because:
options: Partners prefer smaller payments for tax reasons only
It may take considerable time to realise all the firm's assets, and partners should not have to wait until the very end
It avoids the need to prepare a Realisation Account
The law requires at least five separate instalments in every case

questions.q: Under the Maximum Loss Method of piecemeal distribution, at each instalment it is assumed that:
options: All remaining assets will definitely realise their full book value
Only the senior partner will bear any further loss
No further amount will be realised from the remaining assets, and the maximum possible loss is calculated accordingly
The firm will immediately resume normal business operations

questions.q: The Maximum Loss Method ensures that, at each stage of distribution:
options: No partner receives more than what they would be entitled to even in the worst-case scenario
Only secured creditors are paid
Capital accounts are ignored completely
All partners receive exactly equal amounts

questions.q: Under the Proportionate Capital Method of piecemeal distribution, partners are ranked for payment based on:
options: The partner with the lowest capital being paid first, regardless of ratio
The capital each partner has in relation to their profit-sharing ratio, so excess capital is returned before profit-ratio-based distribution begins
The date each partner joined the firm
Alphabetical order of partners' names

questions.q: Under the Proportionate Capital Method, a partner whose capital is relatively higher than what is justified by their profit-sharing ratio is:
options: Never paid until all other partners are fully paid
Paid first, to the extent of such excess, before a general distribution in the profit-sharing ratio begins
Required to contribute additional capital immediately
Excluded from any further distribution

questions.q: Both the Maximum Loss Method and the Proportionate Capital Method are used to ensure that piecemeal payments to partners are made:
options: Randomly, without regard to capital or ratio
Fairly, so that no partner is overpaid relative to their final entitlement
Only to the most senior partner first, in all cases
Only after the business is fully wound up, which defeats the purpose of piecemeal distribution

questions.q: In piecemeal distribution, available cash is first applied towards:
options: Realisation expenses and outside creditors, before any payment to partners
Partners' current accounts only
The insolvent partner's private creditors
Partners' capital accounts directly, before any creditors

questions.q: The concept of "surplus capital" in piecemeal distribution refers to capital that is:
options: In excess of what a partner's profit-sharing ratio would justify, relative to other partners' capitals
Represented by the firm's goodwill
Contributed after the firm's dissolution has been completed
Borrowed by the firm from outside creditors

questions.q: If, under the Maximum Loss Method, a partner's capital account would otherwise go into debit, that excess loss is:
options: Ignored, since the method automatically prevents this situation without further action
Transferred to the Joint Life Policy Account
Charged entirely to the firm's creditors
Reallocated among the remaining solvent partners in their profit-sharing ratio

questions.q: Garner vs Murray is best described as a case relating to English partnership law that has been:
options: Applicable only to companies, not partnerships
Explicitly overruled by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932
Irrelevant to piecemeal distribution
Followed in Indian partnership accounting practice, in the absence of a contrary agreement

questions.q: Insolvency of a partner during dissolution complicates the settlement of accounts primarily because:
options: The insolvent partner automatically becomes the managing partner
All creditors must be paid in shares of the company
The firm's goodwill must be revalued twice
The insolvent partner's share of the deficiency cannot be recovered from that partner

questions.q: When applying the Garner vs Murray rule, the "capital" used for sharing the deficiency is generally based on:
options: The capitals as they stood on the date of the last agreed Balance Sheet before dissolution
The market value of each partner's personal assets
The partners' profit-sharing ratio converted into a capital figure
The partners' drawings for the current year

questions.q: Piecemeal distribution differs from a single lump-sum distribution at the end of dissolution mainly in terms of:
options: The order in which outside creditors are paid
The timing of payments to partners (instalments versus one final payment)
The total amount ultimately payable to partners
The method of valuing goodwill

questions.q: In piecemeal distribution, realisation expenses that are expected but not yet paid are often provided for by:
options: Deducting them from outside creditors' claims
Charging them entirely to the insolvent partner
Ignoring them until the very last instalment
Setting aside an estimated amount before distributing the remaining cash to partners

questions.q: The final instalment in a piecemeal distribution typically results in:
options: The creation of fresh goodwill
The complete closure of all partners' Capital Accounts
The admission of a new partner
The reopening of the Revaluation Account

questions.q: If, under the Maximum Loss Method, a later realisation turns out better than assumed, the partner(s) who received less in an earlier instalment:
options: Permanently lose their entitlement to the difference
Have no further claim on the firm
Receive a correspondingly larger share in the subsequent instalment(s)
Must return part of what they already received

questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes insolvency of one or more partners from insolvency of all partners, in a dissolution context?
options: The latter automatically converts the firm into a limited liability partnership
The former never requires a Realisation Account, while the latter always does
In the former, solvent partners bear the deficiency of the insolvent partner(s); in the latter, no partner can fully absorb the firm's losses
There is no accounting difference between the two situations

questions.q: The Garner vs Murray principle does NOT apply when:
options: The insolvent partner is the most recently admitted partner
The firm has more than three partners
The partnership agreement expressly provides a different basis for sharing such a deficiency
The firm is located outside India

questions.q: On piecemeal distribution, before any amount is paid to partners towards their capital, which of the following must first be fully provided for or paid?
options: The partners' current account credit balances
The firm's goodwill account
Outside liabilities of the firm and realisation expenses
The partners' drawings for the year

questions.q: The practical significance of the Maximum Loss Method is that it allows partners to receive cash:
options: Only if all partners unanimously agree on each instalment amount
Only after a court certifies the complete winding up
Only in equal instalments regardless of entitlement
As soon as it becomes available, without waiting for the complete realisation of all assets, while remaining protected against overpayment

questions.q: When a partner's capital is wholly or partly lost due to a co-partner's insolvency, this loss is shared by the solvent partners as per:
options: The new profit-sharing ratio of an admitted partner
The gaining ratio used at retirement
The firm's audited turnover for the year
Garner vs Murray (or the partnership agreement, if it provides otherwise)

questions.q: In piecemeal distribution problems, the statement showing how surplus capital is returned to partners is prepared mainly under the:
options: Proportionate Capital (Highest Relative Capacity) Method
Garner vs Murray rule exclusively
Admission of a partner procedure
Maximum Loss Method exclusively

questions.q: Under the Proportionate Capital Method, the first partner(s) to be repaid any surplus capital are those with:
options: The highest capital relative to their profit-sharing ratio
The lowest capital relative to their profit-sharing ratio
The shortest tenure in the firm
The highest drawings during the year

questions.q: The underlying objective common to both methods of piecemeal distribution is to:
options: Pay all partners strictly equal amounts at each instalment
Arrive at the same final distribution as a single lump-sum settlement would produce, despite paying in instalments
Eliminate the need for a Realisation Account
Avoid paying outside creditors until the end

questions.q: If an insolvent partner's private estate can pay only part of their personal liabilities, the firm's claim against that estate ranks:
options: Always before the partner's private creditors
Always after the partner's private creditors
Not at all; firms cannot claim against a partner's private estate
Pari passu (equally) with the partner's other private creditors, in proportion to amounts due
